what: The researched pool for the first-launch locals' quiz (GAME_DESIGN 2.6, 12.3): twelve Pacific Northwest questions, each with three answers, the right one and a source. content/quiz/locals.json is built from it in M1a (BUILD_PLAN S15), with the right and wrong lines ("Welcome home.", "Nice try, tourist."). Closes M1A_DATA_CHECK item 23's "source the twelve quiz questions".
rules: Three are dealt per first launch, never two pronunciation questions in a row if a non-pronunciation one is left.
Each question has one true answer, with a source a reader can check.

indigenous_name: true marks place names from the peninsula's and Puget Sound's languages. The quiz asks only how locals say them, never what they mean: meanings need tribal consultation (lore/history.json, consult_before_use).
The creator's own questions are welcome and replace these one for one (GAME_DESIGN, Still to come).
Answer labels fit the 22-character choice cap (F.3).

questions.question: Why do locals call it Sunny Sequim?

source.what: In the rain shadow of the Olympics, Sequim gets under 16 in of rain a year, about as much as Los Angeles; hence "Sunny Sequim". park_rules.json climate gives Sequim 15.8 in.
Pacific Northwest English: "a passage of sunlight in the clouds during dark, rainy weather", typical west of the Cascades.

questions.question: HOH, as in the rain forest, rhymes with:

source.what: The National Park Service gives the pronunciation "hoe".

questions.question: What do hikers call a Canada jay?

source.what: Also known as the gray jay, camp robber or whisky jack; bold at lunch spots (sol_duc_high_divide.json wildlife).
The Pacific geoduck (GOO-ee-duk) is the largest burrowing clam in the world.
Seattle shorthand for a clear day when Mount Rainier can be seen; NASA Earth Observatory notes visitors may hear a local declare "the mountain is out!"

questions.question: Which valley is NOT one of Olympic's rain forests?

source.what: NPS names the Quinault, Queets, Hoh and Bogachiel valleys as the park's temperate rain forests (140-167 in of rain a year).
Pacific Northwest English: jojos, "variation of potato wedges".
